runs.text: Hũs grãosſinhos pretos feios de va-

lines.note: Tōchinkō names small black medicinal pellets. The scan supports grãosſinhos, correcting the corrupt diminutive; feios is retained as printed rather than supplying the tempting t of feitos. The last syllable begins varias on the next row.
Completes varias confeições medicinaes: the pellets consist of various medicinal preparations. The tilde belongs to confeições, and the physical division after va- is retained.
Tochitochito is labelled an adverb and cross-referenced to tochimeki. The Japanese cross-reference begins with a roman T; the OCR incorrectly included that letter inside the italic apparatus.
Qi completes Tochimeqi, followed by its principal form qu. This short physical row finishes the cross-reference and does not constitute a new entry.

runs.text: Cortinas que ſe poem diante do altar, ou

lines.note: Tochō denotes curtains placed before an altar. The caron is visible, and the Portuguese description continues with other places where such curtains are hung.

runs.text: da capella, ou de outro lugar ẽ caſas de nobres.

lines.note: The curtain may also stand before a chapel or another place in noble houses. The abbreviated ẽ is retained without expanding it to em.
Tochū and tochūni are explained by michi no naka, the middle of the road or journey. Latin l introduces the alternative form; neither Japanese phrase is embedded in a Portuguese sentence.
Completes meo do caminho, then allows caminho itself as a gloss. This is a continuation of tochū rather than a separate road-name.
Tōchū is paraphrased as atarashiki chūsetsu, newly rendered loyal service. The visible r in Ataraxiqi corrects the OCR repetition Atataxiqi; the Portuguese feitos is clear here.
The services are newly performed or of the present time. The final upright S. marks written usage and is separated typographically from the italic gloss.
Tokō, with tokaku as the alternative, is adverbial: thus, or in any manner. The divided qual- continues to qualquer below.
Tokō mōsu ni oyobanu means there is no need to speak further in this or that fashion. The negative ending nu is carried over to the next physical row.

runs.text: Não ha pera que falar mais de qualquer

lines.note: Nu finishes oyobanu, and the Portuguese begins the explanation that there is no reason to say more. Its final qualquer continues into maneira below.

After the first translation closes, tokō suru ma ni hi- begins another example, about time passing while one is occupied in miscellaneous activity. The terminal fi- is the first part of the daylight expression continued below.
Ga cureta completes hi ga kureta, the day having grown dark. The Portuguese starts the circumstantial clause about being carelessly occupied, with deſcuidada- divided across the row.

runs.text: mente ſe ocupa aßi, ou aßi, ou em não ſei que

lines.note: Completes descuidadamente and describes being occupied in this way or that, or in something unspecified. The extra s in OCR aßsi is unsupported; both visible expressions are retained as aßi.

runs.text: o ſol ſe pos, ou ſe fez noite.

lines.note: The sun set, or night came: this completes the Portuguese rendering of hi ga kureta. A visible word gap separates ſol and ſe.
Tōkō is explained by hora no kuchi, the mouth of a cave or grotto. Both long-o marks in the headword point upward and are retained as circumflexes.
Toko is a sleeping platform or bedstead, rendered by baileu and catre de dormir. This meaning is distinct from the ornamental alcove platform in the next entry.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de baileu, ou degrao que

lines.note: The second toko is a kind of raised platform or step. The scan has Hũa, not the spurious internal i of OCR Hũia; the relative clause continues below.

runs.text: està na cabeceira do Zaxiqu, onde poem rama-

lines.note: The platform stands at the head of a zashiki, where bouquets are placed. Zaxiqu is a Japanese room-name embedded within the Portuguese gloss; the OCR final a is actually the following comma.
Lhetes completes ramalhetes, bouquets. The brief row closes the alcove-platform description and retains its separate physical line.
Tokogamachi denotes the slats or mouldings of this raised platform. The Portuguese eſ- continues as estão on the next row.

Completes eſ- with the printed-looking tãc, describing mouldings at the platform’s edges. The last letter is open and c-shaped in this impression; although tão is expected linguistically, the aligned OCR tãc is retained with this nonblocking glyph uncertainty.

Tokomushi is a bedbug. The abraded Portuguese gloss is read Perſouejo: a faint inner stroke favours e over the OCR o, but the vowel after P remains uncertain. The historical remaining letters are preserved without substituting modern percevejo.

runs.text: Nome de hũa flor que ſempre hà.

lines.note: Tokonatsu is a flower-name explained through its continual presence. The final mark in hà is a grave rather than the OCR tilde; the statement does not justify imposing a modern species-name.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met, ſe diz de hum homem

lines.note: The entry shifts to a figurative application to a person. Per met is the printed indication of this transferred sense, and the following relative clause supplies its content.

runs.text: que quaſi ſempre està, ou parece da meſma

lines.note: The person is always, or almost always seems, of the same age. The paired verbs being and appearing account for the figurative connection to the ever-present flower.
Idade completes da mesma idade, the apparently unchanging age of the person. It is a genuine short continuation of the preceding figurative definition.
Tokonatsuna and tokonatsuno are alternative adjectival forms meaning constant or unchanging. The next lines explain the property and give trees as an example.

runs.text: ſempre està da meſma maneira ſem ſe mudar,

lines.note: Explains the adjectival forms as always remaining in the same state without changing. The repeated same-manner wording belongs to the definition, not an additional Japanese example.

runs.text: como aruores que lhe não cae a folha, &c.

lines.note: Evergreen trees whose leaves do not fall illustrate this constancy. The historical aruores and singular folha are retained without grammatical modernization.
Toko no umi is a poetic expression equated with namida, tears. P. is the upright poetic-use label; namida is a Japanese explanatory synonym rather than a term inside Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Hũas raizes de erua amargoſas que

lines.note: This tokoro names bitter roots of an herb, not the ordinary noun for a place. The visible u restores erua from OCR eraa; the definition continues with their use as food.
The bitter roots are eaten. This short relative clause completes the botanical entry and must remain distinct from the following homographic headword.
The second tokoro means a place, directly matched by Portuguese lugar. The two adjacent tokoro entries have different senses and are both retained.

runs.text: Por tanto, ou por quanto: por iſ-

lines.note: Tokorode is explained as a consequential or causal connective: therefore, because, or for that reason. The Portuguese iſ- continues as iſſo on the next row.
The gloss also permits sendo aßi, being so; kō aru tokorode supplies the Japanese example. Its caron is retained rather than regularized from modern vowel expectations.

runs.text: Sendo aßi desta maneira, ou por quanto aßi

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the example as things being this way, or because they are so. The latter clause continues to its verb on the next line.
He completes the preceding causal clause, because it is so. The brief ending belongs to the tokorode example rather than to the plural tokorodocoro entry below.
Tokorodokoro means places or each place, preserving both plural and distributive interpretations given by the Portuguese.

runs.text: Penhor que ſe toma noutra terra

lines.note: Tokorojichi is a pledge or distraint taken in another territory. The worn initial has the surviving form of T, and toma corrects OCR Ioma; the next rows specify what is seized and why.

runs.text: de fazenda, ou algũa peßoa que ahi foy ter

lines.note: The pledge can consist of property or a person who has arrived in the other territory. The Portuguese person-word retains the printed ß-type spelling.
The taking of the pledge is occasioned by an injury or a debt. This closes the description of tokorojichi without importing a modern legal definition.

runs.text: He particula como de Datiuo junta

lines.note: Tokoroni is described in the dictionary’s grammatical terminology as a particle resembling a dative. The following line specifies that it combines with verbs.
Mairōzuru tokoroni means when about to go; the prospective form mairōzuru is historical Japanese morphology. Portuguese A- begins Avendo across the physical division.

runs.text: uendo deir, ou estando pera ir me veo ao encõ-

lines.note: Completes Avendo: when obliged or about to go, someone came to meet me. The scan restores uendo, deir and veo ao encõ- from the corrupt OCR sequence; the compressed deir is retained as printed, and encontro continues below.
Tro finishes encontro, and ou me derão adds the alternative that they gave something to the speaker. The line is indented like the preceding continuation, not flush with the headwords.
Tokoshinae and tokoshinaeni express always or perpetually. The historical -naye form is retained rather than modernized to tokoshie.

The gloss adds at all times, then begins a Japanese example using the Christian loanwords Anjo and Ecclesia. The divided Eccleſia- is entirely roman; the OCR’s alternating italic fragments do not match the printed word.
The angels perpetually guard the Church, expressed with the respectful mamoraxeraruru. The object particle uo completes the divided Ecclesia phrase; Os starts the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Anjos ſempre estão guardando a Igreja.

lines.note: Completes the translation: the angels are always guarding the Church. Guardando is one word in the scan; the OCR gap in guar dando is removed.
Tokoyami is lasting darkness, glossed by trevas and escuridade. Xe- begins xecai, the world, in the following example.
Xecai ga tokoyami ni natta describes the world becoming dark. The Portuguese rendering Eſcureceoſe retains the printed historical spelling, and mũ- continues as mundo below.
Do completes mundo; the alternative translation says the world remained in darkness. The short continuation closes the tokoyami example.

runs.text: Premio, ou retribuição das obras que

lines.note: Tokkwa denotes a reward or recompense for actions. The scan restores retribuição and its following word boundary, correcting the OCR retribaiçãodas.

runs.text: hum fez neſta vida, ou noutra idade, ou naci-

lines.note: The actions may have been performed in this life or in another age or birth. The Portuguese naci- begins nascimento across the physical break.
Completes nascimento and attributes the conception to the people the missionary text calls gentios. This closes the explanation of recompense across lives.
Toku and tokutoku are adverbs of speed or earliness. Cedo is divided as ce- and do; the entry is separate from the benefit-sense of toku below.
Toku suru means doing something quickly. The scan clearly has initial T, correcting OCR Focu, and Vt remains italic as part of the apparatus.
Toku means benefit or profit; tokuye begins a related form glossed as profit and personal advantage. The word after the pilcrow is a Japanese subentry, not Portuguese prose.
Intereße proprio completes the explanation of tokuye as one’s own advantage. The printed ligature-like ß is preserved without modernizing the Portuguese spelling.
Tokū is equated with nengu, a payment of yield or revenue. The caron over u is visible and retained even though the preceding homographic toku entry is unmarked.

runs.text: da nouidade das varzeas, ou campos.

lines.note: The payment comes from the new harvest of wet fields or other fields. Novidade here denotes the produce of the season rather than a new fact or novelty.
Tokubun is a share or quantity of benefit. The Portuguese construction continues to identify whose portion is meant.

runs.text: ou ganho que cabe a alguem.

lines.note: The benefit or gain is the amount falling to someone’s share. This continuation supplies the distributive sense of bun in the headword without adding morphological boundaries to the transcription.
Tokudat denotes release or unbinding from sins. Its bare final t is a historical checked coda and is not expanded to a modern syllable in the diplomatic text.
The explanatory i introduces salvar-se, being saved. S. is the upright written-use label; the surrounding Portuguese verb remains italic.
Tokudō is first defined as shaving the head and becoming a religious. The italic Vt introduces the corresponding suru construction.
Tokudō suru illustrates entry into religious life; the additional gloss begins helping others to be saved. The same caron is visible in the repeated Japanese form.
The help toward salvation is given to others through counsel and similar means. This closes the second sense of the preceding tokudō entry.
A separate tokudō entry is paraphrased by michi wo uru, obtaining the Way. Its Portuguese definition begins with understanding the religious law well.

runs.text: dos Fotoques, & as couſas do Buppô, ou ſer

lines.note: The law is that of the hotoke, and the matters belong to buppō. Fotoques and Buppô occur inside the Portuguese explanation and are typeface-toggle candidates; the visible mark on Buppô is a circumflex, not the OCR grave.

runs.text: perfeito, & conſumado no estudo do Buppô.

lines.note: Completes the alternative definition as being accomplished and fully versed in the study of Buddhist law. The final Buppô likewise carries a circumflex, correcting OCR Buppõ.
Tokudō no hito gives the corresponding person: one who understands or is accomplished in these matters. The Japanese phrase itself is an example and is not marked as an embedded Portuguese term.

runs.text: conſumado nas couſas da ley, ou do Buppô.

lines.note: Completes the person’s description as thoroughly versed in the law or buppō. The mark on the final term matches the nearby circumflex forms and replaces the OCR grave.
Tokudōsha is given as equivalent to tokudō no hito. Idem and i form the apparatus linking the compact noun to the preceding descriptive phrase.
Tokuhit is equated with chibifude, a worn-down writing brush. The Portuguese calls it a writing pen; a visible word boundary restores Pena de from OCR Penade.
The writing instrument has a rough and already worn-out point. Tocufit begins the example continued by ni atauazu below; the description explains the humble or inadequate-brush image.

runs.text: Não ſe pode eſcreuer, ou não

lines.note: Tokuhit ni atawazu is rendered as being unable to write it. The Portuguese alternative continues below, explaining the pen’s inability to proceed.

runs.text: pode ir a pena por diante. ¶

lines.note: Completes the explanation that the pen cannot go further. A second expression begins Tokufitni itoma aki arazu; the scan shows ni after the headword, correcting OCR Tocufiti.
Ma completes itoma, and aki arazu closes the second expression. Idem assigns it the same practical sense of being unable to set the matter down; the OCR’s terminal i in Idemi is absent.
Tokuhō is paraphrased by hō wo uru, receiving a law or teaching. The Portuguese extends this to becoming an adherent of a religious law or sect.

Completes the religious-adherence gloss. At the far right the scan also prints the displaced (couſa., omitted by OCR; it completes the following Tocugui definition semantically but remains here on its actual physical row.

runs.text: Proueitos, ou fruito q̃ ſe recebe dalgũa

lines.note: Tokugi is profit or fruit received from something. The final couſa. is printed above at the far right of c2-l036; it is restored there rather than moved into the reading-order sentence. The abbreviated q̃ is retained.
Tokugyō with circumflex is explained by toku no shiwaza, meritorious acts. The Portuguese merito- is divided across the next physical row.
Rias completes meritorias, and proueitoſas supplies beneficial as an alternative. This closes the first of the two adjacent tokugyō entries.
The following Tokuguiǒ has a caron and is glossed as acts of benefit or merit. Both the distinct entry and its different vowel mark are retained rather than merged with the previous headword.

Tokunin and utokunin describe a rich, well-provided person. The restored t joins abastado into its visible word; the provisional st allograph follows the aligned OCR s and is not globally reclassified.

runs.text: Bulle, ou vaſo de barro que tem a bo-

lines.note: Tokuri is a pottery flask or vessel. The definition introduces its small mouth, with bo- continued into boca below.
Ca completes boca, specifying that the pottery vessel has a small opening. This short continuation closes the flask-sense of tokuri.

runs.text: Hum ferro comprido pequeno que ſer

lines.note: The next tokuri is a small, elongated iron tool. The relative clause beginning ſer continues below; no terminal hyphen is supplied where the scan does not show one.

runs.text: ue de cepilho aos carpinteiros menor que o que

lines.note: Ve completes ſerue: the iron serves carpenters as a plane and is smaller than the other tool named on the following line. Cepilho is retained as the printed Portuguese spelling.
The comparison names Sauogana, a Japanese tool-name embedded after Portuguese chamão. It is visibly roman within the otherwise italic explanation and is included among the typeface-toggle terms.
Tokurigana is an alternative name for the same small plane, linked by Idem. The signature and catchword beneath it are page furniture and do not extend this definition.
